national.title: Trump touts imminent decision on potential new attack on Iran
national.summary: President Trump says he will make a decision "very soon" on whether to "destroy what is left of" Iran, calls Qatari emir as mediators push for a peace deal.
national.body: President Trump called Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani to discuss efforts to end the U.S.-Iran war, the emir's office said Friday, amid a diplomatic push to avoid a new round of major hostilities. Their discussion, which the White House had not provided any information about by Friday morning, came as Iran's top diplomat made his own calls Thursday to counterparts across the Persian Gulf aimed at maintaining "stability in the region" amid concerns in many Gulf capitals that Mr. Trump will order major new U.S. strikes. Al Thani received a call from Mr. Trump, according to a statement from the emir's office , during which the pair discussed "the latest regional developments, particularly diplomatic efforts aimed at de-escalating tensions in the region." The emir "emphasized the importance of continuing dialogue and relying on diplomatic means to settle disputes and prevent further escalation," the statement said. CBS/AFP

national.title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader given life sentence for murdering 191 people
national.summary: Paul Mackenzie ordered his followers to starve their children to death in a forest so they could "meet Jesus".
national.body:
A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to life in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.

Alongside 27 others, Mackenzie was found guilty of the murders for instructing members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. The sprawling investigation into the cases shocked Kenya and drew international attention.

Ahead of sentencing, prosecutors in the court in Mombasa had argued for the death penalty for Mackenzie because of the gravity of the crimes.

The prosecutors also cited what they described as Mackenzie's lack of remorse for the crimes. They requested life sentences for his co-accused.

Before the hearing began on Friday morning, Francis Wanje, who lost eight relatives in Shakahola forest, including two grandchildren, told the BBC's Newsday programme that he was "hoping for... a sentence which will match his [Mackenzie's] deeds in the forest".

Mackenzie and the co-accused have formally pleaded for mercy and asked for leniency from the court.

Before their conviction on 19 October, they had all pleaded not guilty and repeatedly insisted that nobody was forced to die.

national.title: Tanzanian opposition leader found guilty of inciting unrest but acquitted of treason
national.summary: The 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, says the charges are politically motivated.
national.body:
Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raised concerns about political freedom in the East African country.

A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam acquitted him of the more serious offence of treason, saying prosecutors had failed to prove a key element of that charge.

But they said the 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, had encouraged his supporters to disrupt the disputed 2025 general election.

Lissu, who leads the opposition Chadema party, has denied the charges, describing the prosecution as politically motivated.

The court said his campaign slogan "No Reforms, No Election" was sufficient for him to be convicted of the charge of incitement.

"By uttering those words with the intention of disseminating them to the public, the accused incited the public to disrupt the 2025 elections," the court ruled.

Lissu said he had only been charged with treason, not incitement.

"The offense of incitement is one that you, honourable judges, have manufactured. You have created an offense that did not exist, and you have done so on political directives," Lissu told the court.

national.summary: Three people accused of using artificial intelligence to impersonate corporate executives and attorneys to steal about $129 million have been indicted, prosecutors say.

Their victims included hospital systems in Missouri and California, a bank in Rhode Island, a financial technology company in the United Kingdom, a mutual fund company in Massachusetts and a pet food company in Florida, according to court documents. The defendants, from Spain, the U.K., Israel and the United Arab Emirates, were also charged with money laundering, according to the indictment. Lawyers for Soall and Sheetrit didn't immediately respond to an email requesting comment. It wasn't clear whether Hazan had an attorney. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York didn't immediately respond to a voicemail left by The Associated Press. The three were arrested between June and September â Soall and Hazan in Spain and Sheetrit in the U.K. Extradition requests for all three are pending.In 2008, Hazan was convicted in a New York court of conspiracy to commit bank fraud, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office. national.title: Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say
national.summary: One child and one young adult were killed in the crash, local authorities say, with more injured.
national.body:
One child and one young adult have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.

The bus was travelling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed at around 07:00 local time on Friday in the town of Lent, around 34 miles (55km) from the border with Switzerland.

The town's mayor Yves Cristin told French media the bus "left the road and hit a tree in the ditch".

The bus was carrying 43 passengers, including 15 children, the Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor's office said. Three people are in a critical condition and a further 13 have sustained minor injuries.

The driver is reported to have been taken to hospital after sustaining injuries and has not yet been questioned by police, the prosecutor's office added.

Local mayor Cristin told BFM TV: "I arrived minutes after the accident and people were in shock.

"The side of the bus was torn off, and clearly, the people who were on that side must have been seriously injured."

Addressing weather conditions at the time of the crash, the mayor told Le Figaro "there was a bit of fog, the road was wet" but there were "no major difficulties".

national.title: Global stocks plunge as fears over US AI slowdown spread to Asia and Europe
national.summary: Investors have reacted to possible tougher scrutiny of data centre construction and the AI industry.
national.body:
Global stock markets have tumbled after investors sold tech shares on fears that the US midterm elections would slow the development of artificial intelligence (AI).

The sell-off, which started in the US and then spread to Asia and Europe, has seen trillions of dollars wiped off the stock value of major tech firms.

In the US, the tech-heavy Nasdaq share index sank 5.5% on Thursday. Asian markets also saw hefty falls on Friday and European markets opened lower.

Investors are worried about tougher regulation of AI, after Democrat candidates opposed the data centres needed by the technology. The share falls also come on top of concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off.

The sell-off in US stocks meant the so-called magnificent seven tech companies, including Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, shed a trillion dollars in value in a single trading day, with Nvidia shares sliding more than 9%.

Shares in Elon Musk's companies SpaceX and Tesla also plunged, falling 8% and nearly 11% respectively and shaving more than $300bn off the firms' market value.

Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday.

The sharp fall in the Nasdaq meant it lost an estimated $2.5tn (£1.9tn) in market value. The index is now in what market watchers call correction territory, which is where an index or company value falls at least 10% below its recent high.

national.summary: The delay in finding the remains of the two women was complicated by difficult terrain and the grizzly bear's behavior.
national.body: Selah Reed's family first knew something was wrong when the 20-year-old missed a routine Saturday night call with her sister. When no one had heard from Reed or her mother, Jenny Balcarras, by the next morning, they asked the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to check on their home in Bella Coola on British Columbia's central coast. Balcarras' car was gone and the doors were locked. They found the car at a trailhead up the road, but Balcarras and Reed were nowhere to be found. Family members across Canada and the U.S. started mobilizing. Jenny Balcarras' brother, Matt, headed north from Vancouver Island, and his brother left from Calgary. They met and drove through the night but got a call late Monday that their sister had been killed, likely by a grizzly. When they arrived at the trailhead Tuesday morning, ready to join the search for Reed, her remains had also been found. The search was now a tragic recovery effort.The killings of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter happened only 3 to 4 kilometers (1.8 to 2.4 miles) from where a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren and teachers last year as they walked on a trail. Eleven were injured, two of them critically, in the Nov. 20, 2025, attack. Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the Conservation Officer Service, said that aggressive bear was never captured, but officials were able to collect its DNA. Officials have set new traps in the hopes of catching the bear involved in last weekend's attack and to learn whether it was the same bear from a year ago. They also are not sure whether more than one bear was involved. Terry Webber, chief administrative officer for the Nuxalk Nation, said the killings were triggering for the families who were traumatized by last year's attack. "Our community is still healing," he said, adding that they've imposed a curfew and are providing mental health services for the community. national.summary: Democrats has proposed a variety of measures aimed at reshaping the Supreme Court over the years and may be poised to push them forward after winning the House and Senate majorities.
national.body: Washington — After years of calling for reforms to the Supreme Court following blockbuster decisions on abortion, presidential power and voting rights, Democrats may be poised to push forward with their court-focused plans after winning control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections. "Accountability begins at home."Jeffries told NBC's "Meet the Press" in August that "dramatic" reform to the Supreme Court is needed, and said Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, who will likely helm the House Judiciary Committee in the next Congress, would take the lead. national.title: Low birth rates were emptying public schools. ICE deportations are now making it worse
national.summary: School enrollment was already expected to plunge by 2 million kids by 2030. Education experts say deporting immigrant families, many with school-age children, is making the crisis worse.
national.body:
Kelly Gonez, a longtime school board member in the Los Angeles Unified School District, says public school enrollment declines worsened after ICE raids escalated in the city in 2025. District officials say low birth rates and the loss of immigrant children in classrooms mean school campuses will likely have to close. Carlos Jaramillo for NPR hide caption

LOS ANGELES — Long before the Trump administration started deporting hundreds of thousands of immigrants, many with school-age children, public schools nationwide faced a massive and accelerating drop in student enrollment caused mostly by shrinking families.

"Birth rates here in Los Angeles County have been declining for decades, which means fewer children enrolled in our schools," said Kelly Gonez, a board member in the LA Unified School District (LAUSD), the second largest in the country, which lost more than 300,000 students over the last two decades.

LA isn't alone. The population of children under age 18 began to fall nationwide after 2010, according to U.S. Census data , dropping by roughly 2.1 million kids through 2025 .

With public schools in much of the country facing a demographic cliff, the Trump administration last year began detaining and expelling large numbers of foreign residents. A study by the Migration Policy Institute found as many as 1.9 million people left the U.S. during the first 18 months of Trump's second term.

As part of the crackdown effort, federal officials weakened restrictions that prevented ICE agents from operating near public schools. "Many of our families immediately went into hiding," Gonez said. "We were predicting a 2% drop in enrollment. It was double that."

Researchers who study education and population trends aren't surprised. This is the first time in nearly a century, since the era of the Great Depression, that birth rates and immigration levels are low at the same time. Large-scale deportations mean even bigger and more rapid changes in areas with large immigrant communities.

"The U.S. isn't alone in facing the challenges of demographic decline," said Thomas Dee, an economist who specializes in education policy at Stanford University. "To stop or slow immigration really exacerbates those problems. Communities are now confronting very painful decisions about closing schools."

national.title: Midterm wave sets a course for "Medicare for All" fight
national.summary: Voter frustration with healthcare costs helped fuel the Democrats' midterm takeover of Congress. But Democratic control doesn't mean "Medicare for All" will follow, as some hoped.
national.body: LANSING, Mich. — Fifteen years working as an emergency room nurse has convinced Kim Bogan that the only way to fix the American healthcare system is to tear it down and start over. Her patients arriving for triage are sicker than ever. They can't afford many of the prescriptions they get in the ER. And sometimes when patients die, she wonders if she could have saved them had she not been caring for five or six other people at once.That's why she spent the past year shuttling between 12-hour shifts at this city's Sparrow Hospital and campaigning for Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat who made "Medicare for All" a signature issue in his congressional campaign and is now a senator-elect. But she realizes that just because progressive candidates successfully campaigned on some form of the policy in states such as Texas, Iowa, Maine, and Michigan, it doesn't mean Medicare for All will be an easy sell. "Nobody expected that," Bogan said. Medicare for All typically refers to a government health program that would guarantee Americans coverage by replacing most or all private insurance. Critics are already pointing out that, even in a blue wave as massive as the 2026 midterms, the most vocal Medicare for All champions generally won by smaller margins than more moderate Democrats."Whatever else people voted for in this midterm election — anger about inflation, anger about corruption, anger about the Iran war — they by and large didn't vote to have the government take over health insurance," said Jonathan Oberlander, a professor and healthcare reform expert at the University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill.Still, supporters of universal healthcare see this moment as a once-in-a-generation opportunity because Americans are buckling under the weight of healthcare costs and are hungry for change. Several states, including Oregon, are already exploring what it would take to set up single-payer systems.The affordability crisis "dominated this election, and Medicare for All speaks to that," Oberlander said. Medicare for All supporters expect the policy agenda will gain major momentum heading into the 2028 Democratic presidential primaries, he said.But more moderate Democrats may see the idea's growing popularity as a threat to gains they made in states such as Iowa, Kansas, and South Carolina. national.title: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
national.summary: Musk said it was to make room for production of its Cybercabs - autonomous taxis without a driver.
national.body:
Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.

He did not spell out whether it plans to stop making them entirely or shift production elsewhere, but did say the decision was to "make room" for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars.

But the project's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest the vehicle was being discontinued, writing on X: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab."

With its distinctive angular looks, the Cybertruck attracted diehard fans, but was beset by delays before being launched in 2023 and has had disappointing sales numbers since.

Tesla fans have been mourning the news online, with one person calling it " the best vehicle Tesla has ever made , external " as he lamented it being "discontinued next year".

Musk responded to the user , external with the word "true", adding: "But the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time."

The vehicle has always been a passion project for Musk. He said it was " way more awesome than people realise , external " in March, and called it the " best product Tesla has ever made to date , external " in April.

But there have always been big questions about whether consumers shared that view and whether the Cybertruck could cut through and earn a spot in the US' lucrative truck market.

Stocks sank across the board, but technology companies with a hand in the AI sector were hit especially hard. The Nasdaq Composite Index tumbled 1,422 points, or 5.5%, to close at 24,315. Dow futures were down 0.8% at 51,192.00. S&P 500 futures gained ground, adding almost 0.3% to 7,402.50. Market watchers think the Democrats' sweeping electoral victories this week could bolster opponents of data centers and slow the rollout of the facilities, which have spurred widespread public opposition. Investors are reacting to the growing "headline" risks around AI, according to Wall Street analyst Adam Crisafulli of Vital Knowledge.The rout was violent enough to potentially delay the highly anticipated initial public offering by Anthropic, a bellwether for the entire AI business, Crisafulli told investors in a research note. Before the turmoil in financial markets, the IPO had been expected to take place this month and to raise as much as $100 billion. The sharp drop also marks a sharp reversal from Wednesday, when the Dow posted its biggest gain of the year. Other indexes also surged after the election results eased uncertainty about who will control Washington."Visible cracks""Even though the market rallied Wednesday after the midterm elections, there were visible cracks in the AI ecosystem, and they widened on Thursday amid investor concerns about a potentially slower data center buildout with Democrats in charge of Congress," Chris Larkin, a managing director of trading and investing for E*TRADE from Morgan Stanley, said in an email.A slowdown in erecting data centers could deal a major blow to AI companies, which are pouring billions into the buildout and banking on widespread adoption of the technology. national.title: U.S. gas prices on track to fall below $4 a gallon, experts say
national.summary: Fuel prices have dropped in recent weeks amid hopes that the midterm elections would increase pressure on the U.S. and Iran to reach a peace deal.
national.body: Motorists could soon see U.S. gasoline prices fall below $4 a gallon for the first time since July, according to energy experts.Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at price-tracking firm GasBuddy, told CBS News that he expects the national average for gas, which the price-tracking firm put at $4.06 a gallon on Thursday, to dip below the $4 threshold by next week. He also predicted diesel could fall below $6 a gallon by Thanksgiving.The average price was still at $4.06 early Friday, according to GasBuddy.Gas and diesel prices have both dropped in recent weeks. The decline was largely due to market expectations that the U.S. midterm elections would underscore public dissatisfaction with the war in Iran and increase pressure on the Trump administration to strike a deal ending the conflict, De Haan said."Oil prices have been falling in the run-up to the election," he said. "My read is because there was optimism that after the midterms these problems would be addressed."Other factors pushing down gas pricesOther factors are also putting downward pressure on fuel costs. Oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has picked up, easing constraints on global oil supply, De Haan said. Brent crude, the international benchmark, fell below $100 on Thursday for the first time since September, trading at $97.44 by midday. West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, was trading at $90.42 a barrel.The recent drop in gas prices is also partly due to seasonal shifts. Prices tend to dip in the fall when Americans pull back on road trips and summer travel, De Haan noted. Filling stations are already switching to winter-blend gas, which is less costly to produce than summer-blend fuel.Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil, predicts that the average U.S. gas price will sink below $4 within the next 10 days. The profit gas stations earn on each gallon of gas sold — currently around 75 cents per gallon — is also larger than usual."Historically, that is too outsized," he said in an email. national.title: After cancer surgery, Pope Leo embarks on Latin America trip
national.summary: Pope Leo XIV is kicking off a three-nation tour of Latin America with a visit to Uruguay, three weeks after undergoing lung cancer surgery that had put the entire trip into question.
national.body:
A mototaxi pass drives past a banner of Pope Leo XIV at Pimentel beach in Chiclayo, Peru, Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, ahead of his planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru from November 6 to 17. Martin Mejia/AP hide caption

ROME — Pope Leo XIV is kicking off a three-nation tour of Latin America with a visit to Uruguay, the region's least Catholic and most secular country, three weeks after undergoing lung cancer surgery that had put the entire trip into question.

Religion Pope Leo's cancer prognosis is 'very good,' according to outside medical experts Leo is due to arrive in Montevideo after a 13-and-a-half hour flight from Rome. He has a packed three-day itinerary in Uruguay including a visit to a neighborhood plagued by gang violence, a Mass in Paysandú, some 375 kilometers (230 miles) from the capital, and another Mass in the city of Florida, about 100 kilometers (60 miles) away.

The Uruguay leg is the first stop on what will be the longest and farthest trip of his pontificate, all being undertaken as the 71-year-old pope continues his recovery. The trip will also bring him to neighboring Argentina and finally back home to Peru, where Leo served as a missionary priest and bishop for two decades.

"His stamina is fantastic. The way that he's singing is incredible. And you can only sing if your lungs are really strong," said Maria Montserrat Alvar, the Vatican's new communications chief. She noted that Leo has passed the 14-day convalescence period required by doctors after his Oct. 13 surgery and is eager to get on the road.

"His doctors are very confident and he'll have plenty of medical care on board should something happen, but we don't see that in his prognosis or even in the way that he's acting," she said.

In Uruguay, which hasn't had a papal visit since 1988, Leo is expected to try to remind the 3.5 million people of their strong Catholic heritage stemming from the times of Spanish colonial rule. He is likely to propose the faith anew as an answer to today's challenges and problems.

Upon arrival, Leo will meet with President Yamandú Orsi, leader of the center-left alliance that assumed power in Uruguay in March 2025, and then deliver his welcome address to government officials and diplomats. He finishes the long day with a vespers service at the city's cathedral.

national.title: Trump signs order to preserve Oval Office as national monument
national.summary: The order comes after Trump made a series of big changes to the decor of the Oval Office and tore down the White House East Wing.
national.body:
US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that he says will prevent future presidents from making certain changes to the White House Oval Office.

The executive order declares the president's official office, which he has renovated, to be a national monument.

"We're making it a national monument, and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Trump told reporters on Thursday.

The order does not prevent future presidents from changing the decor of the famous room.

The document says that it does not "restrict the President's authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character".

American presidents currently have the power to make some changes to the White House but large projects require the permission of Congress.

The order comes months after Trump tore down the entirety of the White House East Wing in a project that has faced legal challenges.

The project was not approved by the US Congress. Construction has continued, with plans to turn the space into a new ballroom.

national.title: Somalia's top court rejects president's term extension amid political crisis
national.summary: The country's first nationwide elections since 1969 are due next year - a timetable now thrown into doubt.
national.body:
Somalia's Supreme Court has ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud unlawfully extended his term, escalating a political crisis and a standoff between the presidency and judiciary.

Thursday's ruling came a day after Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed - a move which the court said the president lacked the authority to take.

The court also ordered political leaders to agree on an electoral plan within 30 days and hold elections within 90 days, potentially disrupting government plans for nationwide polls next year.

Mohamud's four-year mandate expired in May, but his administration extended it by a year through law changes approved by parliament in March.

Opposition groups accuse him of using the constitutional changes to prolong his rule.

But the president insists the reforms are necessary to move Somalia towards fully democratic elections, replacing the clan-based system in which elders pick their representatives.

Somalia last held nationwide direct elections in 1969 and has been wracked by civil war for more than 30 years, with Islamist militant group al-Shabab controlling many rural areas.

Published 24 September 2025 On Thursday, the Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional changes could not be applied retrospectively to the president's current term.

national.title: Melania Trump calls for lasting Ukraine truce as she hosts Russian and Ukrainian officials
national.summary: The US first lady was credited by all for playing a key though unspecified role in the ceasefire.
national.body:
US First Lady Melania Trump called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine as she welcomed Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House following last week's truce in the southern region of Kherson.

Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.

"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.

The unusual White House event saw senior Ukrainian and Russian officials meet away from the setting of official US-brokered peace talks they have been holding without success since last year.

The delegations were made up of Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, as well as Ukrainian MP Davyd Arakhamia and Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev.

The Kremlin envoy also met Donald Trump, the US president later revealed to reporters.

Trump refused to say what they had discussed, but confirmed he had not met the Ukrainian delegation. "There's going to be an agreement," he asserted, "it's going to be a big agreement, and it's going to involve more than Ukraine... and I could even say it might involve all of Europe."

Melania Trump was credited by both delegations at the White House with playing a key though unspecified role in the ceasefire, and all parties conveyed to her the gratitude of the Russian and Ukrainian presidents.

national.title: Major construction ongoing near Iran missile bases, satellite images suggest
national.summary: Evidence of digging and new buildings are visible in satellite imagery taken in November, satellite images suggest.
national.body:
Iran appears to be undertaking significant new construction near at least two of its major missile sites and repairing bases damaged by months of US and Israeli air strikes, analysis of satellite images suggests.

Evidence of digging and new buildings are visible in satellite imagery taken in November at the Garmdareh military base in Karaj near the capital Tehran and the Shahroud base in the north, analysts at British intelligence company MAIAR, who reviewed the photos, told BBC Verify.

At least 12 other military sites, including missile complexes and air bases, appear to show signs of repairs. New roofs have been built on destroyed buildings at the Kermanshah missile base in western Iran, near the border with Iraq, while damaged buildings and debris have been cleared at the Parchin military complex - which has been repeatedly repaired despite a succession of air strikes - east of the capital.

The excavations near Shahroud could potentially be related to the production of missiles, said Jim Lamson, a former CIA analyst who focused on Iran. He said that because the nearby air base at Shahroud has been targeted multiple times in recent years, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) is probably trying to find ways to move its production facilities underground.

A MAIAR analyst said that Iran has "a pattern of moving infrastructure underground to protect them from further strikes". Mark Mellett, a defence analyst and former head of the Irish military, said the construction of underground facilities had the added benefit of making it "harder for outside observers to assess the extent and operational status".

Speculation has mounted in recent weeks that the US could resume attacks on Iran after the midterm elections held earlier this week. But on Wednesday Vice-President JD Vance cited the war's unpopularity with voters for the Republicans' poor performance in this week's poll, saying that it may have cost his party control of the Senate "for the next 6 years".

At multiple bases across the country, Iranian forces have focused on carrying-out small-scale repairs to complexes which have been heavily damaged by air strikes since the start of the US-Israeli war.

Analysts said that satellite images appear to show that significant construction has been completed at the Taleghan 2 facility at the Parchin military complex, with damaged buildings levelled and the aftermath of attacks on an underground bunker repaired and reinforced with concrete.

national.title: Macau jails pro-democracy campaigner in city's first national security case
national.summary: Au Kam San was sentenced to 12 years and six months' jail for "subversion against the political power of the state".
national.body:
Macau has sentenced an ex-lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner to 12 years and six months' jail in the city's first national security case.

Following a closed-door trial, Au Kam San, 69, was convicted on Friday of "subversion against the political power of the state", among other offences.

His wife Virginia Cheang condemned the ruling, calling the case a "groundless persecution designed to humiliate Au".

Macau was handed back to China in 1999, ending over 400 years of Portuguese administration. Its national security law came into effect in 2009, criminalising acts of treason, secession, and subversion against the Chinese Communist Party.

The law was revised in 2023, broadening its scope to include non-violent acts of secession, and again this year, to allow for trials to be held behind closed doors.

Prosecutors had accused Au of assisting and collaborating with "external hostile organisations" by collecting, preparing and disseminating information that was "manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the state".

These took place "over a long period of time", the prosecutors claim.

Au was arrested in July 2025 and later charged with three counts of subverting the state's power, three counts of endangering national security by establishing contact with foreign organisations, and one count of breach of confidentiality.

national.title: Did a data centre revolt affect the US midterm election results?
national.summary: BBC Verify examines whether US voters were influenced by the data centre boom - and the impact anti-AI sentiment could have on the industry.
national.body:
A US midterms voter poll has suggested data centres were a highly motivating issue for many Americans, leading some to argue public backlash against the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure construction boom might have helped shape the election outcome.

BBC Verify has looked at its role in the campaign and examined the potential consequences for the AI industry.

The poll for AP and a consortium of news organisations found 56% of surveyed voters said data centres were a "crucial or major" factor in their vote, while 76% said they would oppose the construction of a new data centre in their community.

The hostile sentiment was considerably stronger among those who said they voted Democrat at this election.

This follows other recent Pew Research polling , external which suggested about half of Americans think data centres are "mostly bad" for the environment, home energy costs and quality of life, a big deterioration in favourability since January.

The congressional voter poll results certainly suggest a remarkable degree of salience for a subject which likely would not have been on most Americans' radar five years ago.

However, it is some way behind several key issues people considered a "crucial or major factor" in their vote, including government corruption (90%) and the cost of living (89%).

Three of the Senate seats flipped by the Democrats have significantly more data centres , external , Texas (595), Ohio (258) and Iowa (117), than the median of 55 across all 50 states.

national.title: A wildfire killed their loved ones in Spain. These British families demand to know why
national.summary: Nine British nationals were among the 15 people who died when fire ripped through the village of Bédar this summer.
national.body:
Relatives of Britons killed in this summer's wildfires in Spain have told the BBC they are disgusted, after regional politicians blocked an official inquiry into the disaster.

Nine British nationals were among the 15 people who died when fire ripped through the hillside village of Bédar, in the province of Almería in south-eastern Spain, on 9 July.

Families have criticised the authorities' actions, including the decision not to send an emergency alert to mobile phones as the flames closed in.

"If that evacuation warning had come through in time, my father would still be alive," says Duncan Chard, who blames failures by officials on the day for a number of the deaths.

The governing People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox in the Andalusian parliament have rejected a request for a commission of inquiry made by the opposition Socialist party to which Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez belongs.

The PP and Vox argued that an ongoing criminal investigation would provide the necessary answers.

The Andalusian government, PP and Vox have been approached for comment.

Families of those killed say there must be a public and transparent probe.

national.body:
A federal judge has temporarily blocked construction of US President Donald Trump's "triumphal arch" in Washington.

US District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled that there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch which the Trump administration had said could begin this week.

Earlier on Thursday the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) voted 8-4 to allow construction of the planned 250ft (72m) arch.

Trump appointees on the board said the arch would be a fitting tribute to US history and to veterans but opponents have argued it would block the view of Arlington National Cemetery, the resting place of thousands of US soldiers and service people.

The so-called Arc de Trump - a play on the name of the famous arch in Paris, the Arc de Triomphe - is one of the US president's efforts to remake the capital city in his style and is meant to commemorate the country's 250th anniversary.

The approval on Thursday evening came after nearly nine hours of public comment.

It is not yet clear when construction of the arch could start, as a number of lawsuits are seeking to block it.

A rendering of the project's design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty statue on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles. The phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" are inscribed in gold on either side of the structure.

local.title: As state moves away from Regents exams, RCSD expands career and college readiness efforts
local.summary: A new statewide framework for high school graduation requirements is in a transition period, and the Rochester City School District is making moves to meet the moment.
local.body:
Listen • 1:18 A new statewide framework for high school graduation requirements is in a transition period, and the Rochester City School District is making moves to meet the moment.

By 2029, public schools across New York will need to assess students' academic performance under the "Portrait of a Graduate" framework.

That model outlines that students must show competency in effective communication, critical thinking, creative innovation, and other academic areas.

At the Rochester City School District, Superintendent Eric Jay Rosser said the district is already shifting focus from Regents exam readiness to capstone project assessments.

"It gives us an opportunity to rethink readiness around what our students truly need for life after graduation,” he said.

Rosser created a new Department of College, Career and Civic Readiness, he said, which will keep track of student participation, and position counselors in secondary schools beginning next year.

"For me, this work comes down to making sure every student leaves us with real options, either a college of their choice, a career of their choice, with opportunities while they're in school to understand the benefits of civic engagement."

The district does not have a public-facing implementation plan for the state-mandated changes, but Rosser said he expects to get more guidance from state officials in the near future.

local.title: Inside MCH’s Friendship Place, rethinking dementia care
local.summary: Plans to redesign Friendship Place, a 25-bed secure unit, began in 2019 with the help of dementia-care expert consultants from around the world.
local.body:
Lydia Cordero had been living at Crimson Ridge Meadows, an assisted living facility, for three years when the 82-year-old started needing more support than the facility could provide.

But with widespread nursing shortages made worse by the COVID pandemic, the number of skilled nursing beds — including those for memory-care patients — has declined across the region and nationally. Her family’s top choices for local memory-care units had waitlists of up to 2 1⁄2 years, according to Lydia's daughter-in-law, Nancy Cordero.

That's when Crimson Ridge suggested the family check out Friendship Place at Monroe Community Hospital.

“When we walked in there, we fell in love with the place,” said Nancy, who toured the recently renovated facility with her husband, Miguel A. Cordero Jr.

“The courtyard was amazing,” she said. “And that's why we picked the room that we did for Mom. Mom is a people watcher, and her room looks right into the courtyard."

Friendship Place is a 25-bed secure unit for residents who may wander, including those with dementia and Alzheimer’s disease. Planning for the redesign began in 2019 — although it stalled when the pandemic hit — with the help of dementia-care expert consultants from around the world. Construction began last year, and the first residents moved in earlier this fall.

It had been decades since its last refresh, and Alyssa Tallo, executive health director at the hospital, said it was time to make some changes.

“We wanted to ... bring it up to a more home-like environment,” she said. “I think someone referred to the (previous) color scheme as ‘Pepto pink.’ It really was outdated. It was not dementia-friendly (based on) what we know now.”

local.summary: Separation anxiety was mightily apparent during a vote in Canada last month. Oil-laden Alberta, which appears more conservative in its values than the rest of the country that proudly waves the maple leaf flag, will not be on its own anytime soon. A referendum that would have created a path toward a
local.body:
Separation anxiety was mightily apparent during a vote in Canada last month. Oil-laden Alberta, which appears more conservative in its values than the rest of the country that proudly waves the maple leaf flag, will not be on its own anytime soon.

A referendum that would have created a path toward a future election and led to possible independence for the province was defeated by a 75% to 25% margin that included more than 1.9 million votes. It is an impressive showing when considering that 5.1 million reside there.

Despite the deflating result, naysayers are not ready to give up the fight. “We’re not going anywhere,” said Jeff Rath of the Alberta Prosperity Project, the Associated Press reported. “We’ve dominated the conversation in the last year. We’ve been educating Albertans on the benefits of independence, and we’re going to continue moving forward.”

It has been a rough couple of years for our neighbors to the north. Not only is animosity brewing from within, U.S. President Donald Trump ruffled feathers by threatening to make the nation our 51st state. He then began a trade war that has harmed relations between the border nations who were once seen as being best of friends.

Retaliation, however, has been swift and painful. Many from the North are choosing to travel elsewhere, impacting tourism in parts of Western New York that include Chautauqua Institution. They're also being more global, looking to expand and grow economic partnerships with European countries.

In Canada, when the relations with the U.S. became precarious, leadership looked across the Atlantic Ocean. They kept their options open.

That brings us to the major rift within New York: upstate and downstate.

This week's election proved again that portions of rural, red-leaning regions still have very little clout in an entity that is dominated by New York City and metropolitan counties that include Erie, Monroe, Onondaga and Albany. Through an Assembly and Senate that leans far left, policies that are driven by those living downstate continue to hamper our way of life.

local.summary: As deer hunting season begins to hit its stride across Western New York, the valleys of southern Chautauqua County, particularly those near the Pennsylvania line, have already been feeling the bite of autumn. Frost-covered pumpkins and a string of chilly mornings, despite our overall warming trend,
local.body:
Submitted Photo Clint Catchot used a Mathews Lift-X bow set at 75 pounds draw weight, topped with a Grim Reaper Pro broadhead to take home this giant deer last week in Southern Chautauqua County.

Submitted Photo Big Chautauqua County deer are not new for 33-year-old Clint Catchot, who credits his Uncle Craig Silleman with getting him started in hunting when he was 12-years-old.

As deer hunting season begins to hit its stride across Western New York, the valleys of southern Chautauqua County, particularly those near the Pennsylvania line, have already been feeling the bite of autumn. Frost-covered pumpkins and a string of chilly mornings, despite our overall warming trend, signal a change in the woods. For some hunters, the early cold snaps can mean an early turn in the whitetail rut.

For 33-year-old Clint Catchot of Perrysburg, the timing couldn’t have been better. Catchot is a seasoned hunter who has already taken his share of impressive bucks, but recently experienced what every deer hunter hopes will happen someday: an encounter with the biggest buck of his life. The result was a remarkable 153-inch whitetail (estimated green score) taken from a treestand on a permission property in southern Chautauqua County.

Catchot had hung the stand just one day before the hunt. After seeing a few does and a smaller buck that first evening, he decided to return the following morning. It was a decision that would make for a hunt he won’t soon forget. The morning started with a little mishap when he dropped his grunt call and backpack from the tree. Mother Nature and the woods had other plans.

“Ten minutes later I saw a doe and a fawn. Ten minutes after that the buck came through 70 yards down wind,” Catchot recalled. The buck was moving cautiously, taking his time and seemingly checking every inch of his surroundings. He uses grunt calls from time to time.

“Very slow and cautious. He would walk 10 yards then look around for a minute or two. Then walk 10 more yards and do it again.”

It was a test of patience. With his experience, Catchot knew better than to rush the moment. Eventually, the buck worked his way to inside 35 yards, offering a broadside opportunity.

local.body:
Students from SUNY Fredonia will be doing their part to contribute to their community this weekend. Fredonia's annual Fall Sweep is this Saturday beginning around noon throughout the village.

Fall Sweep is an annual volunteer initiative where SUNY Fredonia students partner with the Village of Fredonia to assist residents with seasonal yard cleanup, leaf collection, and neighborhood beautification. The event is one of SUNY Fredonia's largest civic engagement events, bringing together hundreds of students to support local homeowners and strengthen campus-community connections.

"It's a really fun event and I really appreciate the community for letting us do this every year. It means a lot to the campus to be able to go out and do it, and I'm sure it means a lot to the community too," said Syd Smith, Chair of Community Relations through the Student Association at SUNY Fredonia.

Various student clubs participate in the event, where they are each assigned a street in the village. Homeowners in the village hang fliers on their door if they wish to participate, and on the day of the event, students stop by to rake leaves and clean the lawn. The event usually lasts roughly two hours before students meet back on campus for a reception.

Fall Sweep began roughly two decades ago. It was previously coordinated by the student-run Applied Communication Association, but last year, Smith took over coordinating the event as a freshman at Fredonia. The Applied Communication Association is assisting this year under Smith's direction.

"It was definitely a lot to handle as a freshman with not a lot of experience with the campus at all. I was kind of thrown into it, but I honestly wouldn't have had it any other way," Smith said.

Roughly 300 students participated in last year's event. Now in her second year running things, Smith hopes for another successful event this weekend with 17 clubs signed up to participate.

"We had a great turnout last year. It was amazing. I couldn't have asked for a better turnout for my first year," Smith said.

The Patterson Library will host a special historical presentation by author Mary Ellen Humphrey at 5:30 p.m. Thursday. The discussion will focus on Mercy Otis Warren and her influential, multi-layered role before, during, and after the American Revolution, drawing from the author’s compelling book, "Corresponding With Marcia."

Warren was one of the most formidable political writers and propagandists of the Revolutionary era, utilizing her sharp wit and extensive correspondence to shape early American political thought. The presentation will explore her life, her amazing contributions to the fight for independence, and her enduring legacy as a historian of the Revolution.

“Mercy Otis Warren’s voice was vital to the foundation of American liberty, yet her full impact is often left in the shadows of the Founding Fathers,” said Mary Ellen Humphrey, author of Corresponding With Marcia. “This presentation aims to reveal her brilliant role in the Boston Tea Party, and the adoption of the Bill of Rights to our constitution, and much more. We've heard history. This is her story.”

The event is free and open to the public. It will take place in the community room at the Patterson Library, located at 40 S Portage St, Westfield, NY 14787.

For more information about the event or to reserve a seat, please visit the Patterson Library website atpattersonlib.org or call (716) 326-2154.

Humphrey is an author and educator. "Corresponding With Marcia" is the culmination of extensive research into the personal works and political influence of this woman during the American Revolution.

local.title: LIV Golf tells bankruptcy court it will wind down operations
local.summary: LIV Golf is shuttering after five years that fractured the sport’s landscape with promise of Saudi riches, announcing Thursday in bankruptcy court it plans to wind down operations instead of launching a new version because it didn’t have enough support. “The debtors are not currently proceeding with
local.body:
LIV Golf is shuttering after five years that fractured the sport’s landscape with promise of Saudi riches, announcing Thursday in bankruptcy court it plans to wind down operations instead of launching a new version because it didn’t have enough support.

“The debtors are not currently proceeding with the LIV 2.0 plan,” attorney Matthew Williams of Gibson Dunn said in a hearing in New Jersey. “Instead, the debtors are toggling to a value-maximizing wind-down in their business.”

LIV Golf, which launched in June 2022 by offering nine-figure signing bonuses to lure top names away from the PGA Tour, lost Saudi Arabia funding in April after spending more than $5 billion.

It filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on Sept. 8 and thought it had a lifeline in BC Partners Credit, which pledged a $300 million investment to pivot to a more financially sustainable “LIV 2.0.” But players like Jon Rahm and Sergio Garcia, Tyrrell Hatton and Louis Oosthuizen, weren’t interested.

“BC Partners Credit supported a transaction that aligned the interests of players and investors, offering a credible path toward building a sustainable future for LIV Golf,” BC Partners said in a statement. “While there was great support for the league, we are disappointed that mutually acceptable terms could not be reached among the various stakeholders.”

Instead of planning for a new version for 2027, LIV enters a liquidation phase.

Rahm already agreed to forfeit all claims against LIV -- said to be worth some $100 million -- to get out of his contract. He is back to playing the European tour, with hopes there will be a path back to the PGA Tour. The tour currently has a one-year ban dating to players’ last LIV appearance.

LIV Golf paid $15.6 million to retain seven of its executives, including $6.375 million to CEO Scott O’Neil, in the months between the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia and LIV filing for bankruptcy. Those payments are not unusual for a company trying to emerge from bankruptcy. The question now is whether those payments can be voided since LIV isn’t going forward.

local.title: Economy growing, purchasing power is not
local.summary: The economy is strong by conventional measures, but most voters don’t feel it. Gross domestic product grew 3.4 percent in the third quarter, the fastest pace in a year. Consumer spending increased 3.8 percent, and nonresidential business investment surged 12.7 percent, propelled by artificial intell
local.body:
The economy is strong by conventional measures, but most voters don't feel it. Gross domestic product grew 3.4 percent in the third quarter, the fastest pace in a year. Consumer spending increased 3.8 percent, and nonresidential business investment surged 12.7 percent, propelled by artificial intelligence and the data center build-out.

At the same time, the final Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll before the midterms found that 75 percent of Americans describe the economy as poor or not so good. Forty-eight percent say they're financially not as well off since President Donald Trump took office, more than three times the 15 percent who say they're better off. Fewer than 3 in 10 Americans approve of how Trump is handling the economy.

Democrats are favored to flip the House on Tuesday and have a real chance to capture the Senate. Persistent inflation, more than anything else, explains why the party in power is not receiving more credit for economic growth, low unemployment, deregulation, stock market gains and historic levels of capital investment.

Inflation has been a problem since Washington pumped trillions of dollars in stimulus into the economy during the covid pandemic. While inflation has cooled from its 9.1 percent peak in 2022, Trump has contributed to rising prices with unnecessary tariffs, an overzealous immigration crackdown and the Iran war, which has raised energy costs.

Inflation is a corrosive stealth tax that makes people feel like they're not getting ahead. Average hourly earnings rose 3 percent over the past year, but consumer prices climbed 3.7 percent. As a result, real hourly earnings fell 0.7 percent. Gasoline jumped 9.1 percent in September and is now 34.2 percent more expensive than a year ago.

No wonder affordability is front and center. Nearly two-thirds of campaign ads in competitive races last week mentioned the economy.

The squeeze is especially acute in districts that will determine House control. A Post analysis last week found that 6 in 10 families cannot afford the basic cost of living in the 46 most competitive districts. Between 2019 and 2024, median costs rose 33 percent while median incomes rose 28 percent. Incomes failed to keep pace with costs in 42 of the 46 districts.

Trump won in 2024 by promising relief from those pressures. Some of his policies are instead aggravating them. Take tariffs. Federal Reserve researchers found that tariffs imposed in 2025 raised core goods prices 3.1 percent through February. Yale's Budget Lab estimated that the tariffs in place over the summer would raise consumer prices about 0.7 percent, costing the average household roughly $1,100 annually.

Steve St. George was, in fact, granted a special use permit to operate a concrete and asphalt recycling yard at a property he owns in the town. At the third Zoning Board hearing regarding the project, held in October, the Board granted the permit with a list of conditions attached.

A previous OBSERVER article erroneously reported the project was still awaiting approval, citing Zoning Board discussions held in October 2025 -- the first of three hearings -- rather than the most recent discussions held in October 2026, as the project received approval.

On Oct. 6, the Town of Pomfret Zoning Board of Appeals granted St. George a special use permit for recycling operations at 3624 Webster Road, Fredonia. The property was formerly used for grape vineyards.

St. George operates S. St. George Enterprises, a construction company that often works with roadways in the region. St. George sought a permit to recycle the materials from his company on site. Initially, a building permit at the site was denied because the use was not defined under the zoning code's acceptable uses.

Members of the Zoning Board recently conducted a site visit, during which the equipment was run at full speed and volume. The decibels were measured and the readings did not pass the threshold to require ear protection. Chairman David Fridmann spoke with the Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC), who provided documentation that authorized the operations until 2031. The DEC will continue to monitor the project.

The Zoning Board was required to evaluate the project under the State Environmental Quality Review Act guidelines. The Board issued a negative declaration, meaning that the project does not negatively impact the environment.

In granting St. George approval, the Zoning Board restricted operation of recycling equipment to weekdays between 7:30 a.m. and 4 p.m., aside from delivery or transport from the site. Operation of recycling equipment is restricted to 50 days annually. If the operations grow in scale to require more than 50 days annually, another special use permit application must be filed.

The September hearing featured objections from roughly a dozen residents in attendance from the community neighboring the site. Residents shared concerns with noise, dust, well water contamination, hours of operation, and lighting. The Board also highlighted concerns with environmental impacts.

local.body: Crews are nearing the final stages of restoration work on the iconic dome of the Basilica of Our Lady of Victory in Lackawanna.Monsignor David LiPuma said the restoration is nearly 80% finished, with fall weather allowing crews to make headway before winter."It's been beautiful," Monsignor LiPuma said. Crews are preparing to remove its copper and install a protective covering for the winter months.Monsignor LiPuma said the temporary covering allows the team to monitor how it performs through the winter before returning in the spring to replace the copper and continue work on the dome.WATCH: Restoration of Our Lady of Victory Basilica dome nears completion in LackawannaCrews are expected to continue working in December, weather permitting, before taking a winter break.The current timeline calls for the restoration, including the cupola, to be completed in July 2027. local.title: Rochester's high housing costs stand in the way of a new safe house for women fleeing domestic violence
local.summary: Willow is seeking to build a safe dwelling for those fleeing domestic violence. The biggest barrier standing in the way are Rochester's high housing costs.
local.body:
The Willow Domestic Violence Center is setting out to purchase a safe dwelling house in Monroe County for women fleeing domestic violence.

But it's hit a snag: a housing market that is simply too expensive and competitive.

"I think it's more of a supply and demand thing," Nicole Morelle, chief impact officer at Willow, said. "There's very little supply, a very high demand, and if we had more housing, it would be more affordable, and we would be able to meet the needs of everyone that called our hotline instantaneously."

The lack of safe dwellings or other suitable housing for people fleeing domestic violence has resulted in a constant waitlist of well over 100. In late October, there were 104 women on the waitlist.

Willow operates a 49-bed shelter in Monroe County, with the rest of the shelters or safe dwellings for women fleeing domestic violence scattered around the nine-county region. In total, there are 94 beds available for women fleeing domestic violence in the region.

When there are no other options, clients are often put up in hotels. That is costly and not ideal for creating a safe environment for recovery, said Willow officials. The only option beyond those resources are homeless shelters.

"The need for beds is so significant that as we're grappling with this, we're hearing from survivors, we're hearing from partners, we're hearing from the community," said Meaghan de Chateauvieux, president of Willow. "We know this for ourselves, there are not enough beds."

Toi Walker-Smith, director of supportive housing for Willow, said high rental and home purchasing prices are almost entirely to blame for Willow's dilemma.

entertainment.title: Interscope Expands Into Brazil With Hip-Hop Artist BK, Supernova Entertainment Joint Venture
entertainment.summary: The new twin deals portend the label's significant expansion into the eighth-largest music market in the world, according to IFPI.
entertainment.body:
Interscope Records is branching out into Brazil, the company announced Friday (Nov. 6), unveiling two new deals in the country: the signing of hip-hop star BK, and a new joint venture/distribution deal with leading urban label Supernova Entertainment.

For BK, signing with Interscope coincides with the 10th anniversary of his debut album, Castelos & Ruinas ; his first release for Interscope will be a remix of that album with new production and new collaborations. The new JV with Supernova encompasses the Brazilian urban label’s catalog and a partnership for new signings.

“We have shown through our successful track record over the past few years that wherever they come from, artists are attracted to the kind of global artist development platform we can provide at Interscope,” Interscope Capitol Miami executive vp/GM Jose Cedeño said in a statement. “Having BK as our first artist signing and Supernova as our first label deal, illustrate how serious our mission is to empower Brazilian artists to become global superstars.”

The Brazilian market has been a particular focus of the majors in recent years — one that reflects both investment in the country itself and the subsequent growth in subscription streaming and consumption in general. In March, IFPI reported that the Brazilian music market had grown by 14.1% year over year, much higher than the 6.4% growth of the industry overall, jumping over Canada to become the eighth-largest market in the world.

“Brazilian music and culture are having an extraordinary impact around the world right now,” Interscope Capitol chairman/CEO John Janick said in a statement. “We see an opportunity to leverage our legacy and current success in urban music for important Brazilian artists like BK and labels like Supernova Entertainment. We are excited to expand the resources and opportunities for Brazilian artists to move culture on a global level.”

Those opportunities were expanded upon by Victoria Oakley, IFPI’s CEO, in a new interview with Billboard this week. “I think we’re seeing the music economy emerge at the same time as we’re seeing the Brazilian economy emerge,” Oakley said. “It’s also a place of phenomenal talent, and their export story is much more successful so far, principally across their own region. But I think given that most of the music is in Portuguese and not in Spanish, so the obvious sellable market isn’t there in quite the same way, they’ve done a phenomenal job with their export story and they are on the increase. They too have a government that I think, from early on, places culture as an important part of the education system, and I think that is quite an important first step that we often don’t see the benefits of until much later.”

entertainment.title: “Saviors of Cinema” and “Money Machine”: Tallinn Puts Spotlight on Kids, Youth Films and Social Media Bans
entertainment.summary: Kärt Väinola, the head of the Just Film Industry Days, taking place during the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival, also previews how AI and labels will be debated during its fourth edition.
entertainment.body:
Estonia’s Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival ( PÖFF ) kicks off its 30th anniversary edition on Friday. In addition to latest art house discoveries, movies for younger audiences will also take the spotlight at the event – as has become tradition.

PÖFF launched its popular Just Film Festival for youth and children’s movies in 2001. Since 2023, it has also organized the Just Film Industry Days to provide networking, education and pitching opportunities for people working in or looking at the space.

During the 2026 edition of the Black Nights festival, running Nov. 6-22, the Just Film Industry Days event takes place Nov. 18-20. It is an initiative by the Industry@Tallinn & Baltic Event strand of PÖFF and its Just Film Festival, which will this year screen the likes of Rebekah Fortune’s Learning to Breathe Under Water , Zane Borg’s River , David Dietl’s Emil and the Detectives , and Thomas Mendolia’s Henry’s Ebb . Attendees can expect two and a half days of pitching sessions, panel talks, case studies, presentations and more for people involved or interested in films and media content for children and young audiences. “We love quality films for children and young audiences,” the kids and youth strand’s website highlights – and invites people. “That’s why we welcome people working in film production – directors, producers as well as other creatives, who’ve already made children’s and youth films and/or are currently working on one, looking for partners at different stages, or are simply seeking like-minded people. Even if you’re just considering pursuing a film project for children or youth, this is the place for you.” Related Stories Business Dark Slope to Open New Virtual Production Stage in Vancouver (Exclusive) Movies 'The Wizard of Oz' Was a Big Reference for Doc 'A Want in Her.' Now Its Creator Is Moving Into Fiction.

Kärt Väinola is the head of Just Film Industry Days, along with serving as Baltic Event Co-Production and International Works in Progress co-manager, Just Film Works in Progress manager and panels & talks coordinator.

She talked to THR about why Tallinn has been proudly putting the spotlight on kids and youth content, how it fits into broader industry trends and why social media bans, whether launched and considered, will be among the hot topics of discussion this year.

This is Väinola’s 22nd year working for the festival and her fourth year on the four-year-old Just Film Industry Days section. “Organically, it just grows and grows and grows,” she says. “We now have two pitching events together with the co-production market, focused on Just Film projects in development or early production and works in progress.”

QOTSA leads the latest chart with Perfecth , their ninth studio album . It’s the seventh top 10 appearance for Josh Homme and Co., and their third leader after 2013’s … Like Clockwork and 2017’s Villains . Perfecth is the best seller on wax for the week, earning top spot on ARIA’s Vinyl Chart.

Canadian rock favorites Nickelback start on the chart podium with Everything Under The Sun (Virgin Music Group/Inertia), their 11 th studio album. It’s new at No. 3. Australian actor, singer and comedian Eddie Perfect enjoys a career-best result with Beetlejuice (Live At The Regent Theatre Melbourne) , which opens its account at No. 5 on the latest chart, published Friday, Nov. 6. Indeed, it’s a first-ever appearance in the top 50 for Perfect, who reprised the title role last year in the Australian production of Beetlejuice The Musical .

Close behind is Aussie country artist Fanny Lumsden , whose new album Traditions debuts at No. 6 on the ARIA Chart. That’s Lumsden’s third consecutive top 10 appearance and a new career high. Traditions is the fifth studio album for Lumsden, a two-time ARIA Award winner.

Gretta Ray has her own career high with Heartsong (EMI), the Melbourne-born singer and songwriter’s third studio album. It’s new at No. 11, besting the peak of her 2021 debut Begin To Love Around , and the No. 17 best for 2023’s Positive Spin. It’s an uplifting comeback for Ray, who endured a five-week hospital stay in 2024 after falling ill with “severe” cardiac disease — infective endocarditis, a rare and life-threatening ailment that can cause damage to the heart.

entertainment.title: Pamela Abdy Gets Real About Her “Pure, Unadulterated Rage” in WIF Honors Speech: “What Business Are We Leaving?”
entertainment.summary: The former Warner Bros. exec gave a passionate 15-minute speech at the event, where she was presented with the Vanguard Award.
entertainment.body:
Pamela Abdy made her first public appearance since she and Mike De Luca were outed at Warner Bros ., stepping out at Women in Film ‘s annual WIF Honors event on Thursday — where she did not hold back.

The exec received the inaugural Vanguard Award, a recognition for a leader whose career embodies the qualities that move the industry forward, presented by Nancy Meyers. The honor was announced before her exit from the legacy studio, which took place as Paramount Skydance completed its $111 billion merger with Warner Bros. last month. Related Stories Business Pam Abdy Laments Exits of Top Female Executives in Hollywood: "It Is Upsetting to See" Movies John Mulaney Teases His 'Get Smart' Reboot: "My Favorite Type of Person to Play"

Taking the stage, Abdy reflected on how she has worked with some of the greatest filmmakers of all time and tried to make films that spark “valuable conversations and debate.” However, she continued, “We also have to do this under the microscope of a media ecosystem that has largely abandoned analysis and fact for the trap of clickbait.” The exec then ran through a list, thanking every female director she has produced or worked with to date, followed by lists of the female execs and producers.

“My gratitude for these women has only grown over the years, but lately other feelings, and one in particular, have risen to the surface with undeniable ferocity — and that feeling is pure, unadulterated rage,” she told the crowd inside the Beverly Hilton. “Rage for these women, rage for me, and even more rage for the entire generation of women who deserve to have their potential recognized and elevated. Rage at how women are under attack everywhere. Rage at how our health and our well-being always seem to come second to how we show up in a room, and here’s the problem: as a leader who happens to be a woman, I am supposed to sublimate this rage. And you know what happens when they tell you to tamp down a fever? Sometimes it just burns hotter.”

Abdy continued, “I’ve been called difficult, emotional, combative. I’ve been told to put on my big-boy pants, to smile more. I’ve been told movies starring women and movies directed by women don’t make as much money, that the audience is limited. That everyone gets nervous when our sisters lead a movie because traditional tracking suggests men won’t show up,” going on to call out male directors for not supporting female directors in the same way they support each other.

This week, Lil Baby is back with his anticipated fifth album; JENNIE drops a new single for the animated Netflix film STEPS ; Dove Cameron releases her long-awaited debut album; and Boys Noize returns with his first solo studio album in five years.… plus much more.

After scoring his third consecutive Billboard 200 No. 1 album with WHAM last year, Lil Baby is gunning for his fourth with Fresh . The new set arrives with a title inspired by his recent hit single “Dead Fresh,” an infectious, Pharrell-produced joint that soared to No. 18 on the Billboard Hot 100 and topped Rhythmic Airplay. Stacked with guest appearances by frequent collaborators Future, Young Thug and Rylo Rodriguez, Fresh finds Baby delivering 17 new songs that reassert his position as one of the most gifted mainstream MCs to blow up this decade. — KYLE DENIS

The inviting disco-colored intro of “Someone To Hold” neither sounds like a typical song for JENNIE nor a Disney princess — and that’s what makes it magic . The colorful pop song shows a new side of JENNIE’s artistry that leans more playful and vibrant than anything on her solo debut full-length, while also matching the fresh take of the movie it’s from — as the upcoming musical comedy Steps reimagines Cinderella from the perspective of the stepsisters. — L.H.

Despite launching her career over a decade ago in Disney TV and film franchises — also lending her voice to both — Final Girl is Dove Cameron’s debut full-length. At long last. The dramatic and soaring album delivers a range of tempos and emotions, from softer songs like pop ballad “Silver Screen Baby” and the raw “Immortalized” to uptempo dance-pop single “When In Rome” and the haunting and heavy “Skin On Bone.” It’s an album that was well worth the wait, and offers so much possibility and intrigue as to what sounds and styles Cameron will want to explore next. — L.H.

On it, she sings: “After, after everything that we’ve been through / The ins and outs, the upside downs and good times too / You’re still the shooting star that’s in my skies / You’re still the only one I want in every life.”

Tranter, who wrote and produced three more original songs for the film’s official soundtrack, has described “Someone to Hold” as “pure danceable joy inspired by vintage organic dance pop.”

Directed by Alyce Tzue and John Ripa, Steps sends the tale of Cinderella in a different direction. According to a statement, Cinderella’s “evil” stepsisters Lilith (Ali Wong) steals the magic wand belonging to the Fairy Godmother (Bette Midler) and hijacks the Royal Ball with Margot (Stephanie Hsu). Enter Priscilla (Nikki Glaser), a “villainous schemer who swoops in and snatches the throne.” With Priscilla in charge, consider the party over. And the happily-ever-after ending ruined.

Realizing her terrible move, Lilith must join forces with Cinderella (Amanda Seyfried) in an epic quest, with battles royale and friendships forged along the way.

entertainment.title: ‘It Would Take a Lot to Say No to Australia’: Foo Fighters Kick-Off Tour Down Under With Three-Hours of Power
entertainment.summary: The Foos were back on familiar turf for their Take Cove r Australian tour opener at Suncorp Stadium in Brisbane, the noisy neighbor to the XXXX brewery.
entertainment.body:
Australia is at the mercy of factors beyond anyone’s control. Extreme weather, the tyranny of distance. This great southern land is at the ass-end of the world, a journey that that will take many travelers a day out of their life to get there, and another to return home.

In rocks the Foo Fighters , again, urging you to hold their beer. In January of this year , the U.S. band completed the long-haul for a one-off show in Launceston, the second city of Tasmania, an island some 1,600 miles north of Antarctica. On that occasion, the Foos spent 48 hours traveling, for a three-hour show at UTAS Stadium. Mission accomplished. Four years earlier, in 2022, Dave Grohl and Co. performed for one-night only at GMHBA Stadium in Geelong, a satellite city of Melbourne, to help refuel a touring industry crippled by the lockdown.

On Thursday night (Nov. 5), the Foos were back on familiar turf for their Take Cove r Australian tour opener at Suncorp Stadium in Brisbane , the noisy neighbor to the XXXX brewery. It’s their second visit to this country in 10 months. In a quirk of the schedule, the band will break after the Adelaide date on the tour, Nov. 17, and return in late January for New Zealand shows and a tour closer in Perth. Count them. That’s three visits to Australia in a year, all of them for concerts produced by Frontier Touring.

The Foos love Australia, and it’s reciprocated. Guitarist Chris Shiflett stepped out wearing an AC/DC shirt, with the sleeves hacked off. Grohl recounted his three-decade-long affair with the country, before the band played “Big Me” from their self-titled 1995 debut album. The parody “Footos” music video, Grohl revealed, was shot here. The Foos might as well have Aussie passports at this point.

“I’m so f—ing grateful, and lucky, that we’re still here 30 years later, and coming to tour for you guys again,” Grohl told his audience. “It would take a lot to say no to Australia.”

From the gritty staccato chords of “All My Life” and Grohl’s “are you f—ing ready” pep talk, through to the Foos’ traditional ending number “Everlong,” Billboard soaked up the action on a glorious spring night.

There’s no mystery to a Foo Fighters show. You know what’s coming. Stadium rock, old favorites, hits, energy. It’s a meal that’s both nutritious and heavy enough that you don’t leave hungry.

The Rock Hall-inducted band paid it back to Generation X, the “old school,” many of whom were in the crowd, with their kids along for the ride. The first 10 songs was a greatest hits set, opening, as the Foos do, with “All My Life.” One by one they knocked them down. “The Pretender, “Times Like These,” “Rope,” “Stacked Actors,” My Hero,” “Learning to Fly.” These guys don’t come down to land.
